overview: This Sardinia record covers the island kingdom under the Spanish crown during 1530 to 1700. Sardinians lived with local institutions, maritime dangers, religious learning and recurring epidemics. The island-shaped outline is reasonable as a regional frame; its dates are a map window within a much longer history.

periods.title: Sardinia under the Spanish crown
periods.summary: The island belonged to a wider monarchy while retaining its own institutions and communities.

sections.title: Government, defence and getting an education

items.text: Sardinia’s parliament had three estates, or stamenti: clergy, nobles and representatives of the seven royal towns. It negotiated taxes and proposed legislation for royal approval. This gave organized groups a bargaining role, but was not an assembly elected by every adult on the island.

In Cagliari, the estates could meet in different buildings: church representatives at the archbishop’s residence or cathedral sacristy, nobles at the church of the Speranza, and town representatives at the municipality. Delegates carried messages between them and the viceroy. Government involved plenty of walking as well as talking.

Philip II established the Royal Administration of the Towers in 1587 to organize coastal defenses, soldiers and supplies. Guards watched for hostile ships. For coastal communities threatened by raids, keeping watch over the sea was a serious, organized job.

A tower’s entrance could stand about four to six metres above the ground. Guards reached it by a wooden or rope ladder and then pulled the ladder inside. Reaching the rooftop lookout could require another ladder through a hatch or stairs built into the thick walls.

Early-sixteenth-century Cagliari and Sassari supported public grammar schools. Language could be political: in 1567, Philip II required the Jesuits at Sassari’s college to use Castilian in teaching and even in preaching in the city. Local elites wanted their sons to master it alongside their humanistic studies.

Cagliari’s university received papal authorization in 1607 and a royal foundation privilege in 1620; arrangements for teaching were still being implemented in 1626. The proposed funding split costs between church and city. Establishing a university meant finding rooms and money as well as signing an impressive parchment.

The papal authorization envisaged subjects including medicine, law, philosophy and Latin, Greek and Hebrew. In the royal arrangements, Cagliari’s council would select the rector for a three-year term, while the archbishop could confer degrees. These documents reveal how civic and church authorities shared responsibility for higher learning.

sections.title: Books and a small sample of Sardinian

items.text: Nicolò Canelles established a printing shop in Cagliari in 1566. Copies preserved in the University Library document this early local printing enterprise. Books could now be produced on the island through a durable workshop, adding a new craft to its cultural life.

Gerolamo Araolla’s collection of 1597 mixed Sardinian, Italian and Spanish poetry. Its original printed heading includes “RIMAS DIVERSAS SPIRITUALES”, meaning “Various spiritual poems”. This is a transcription of an attested title, recorded by the modern editor from the surviving Cagliari copy, not a newly composed example of Sardinian.

sections.title: Families, illness and evidence from teeth

items.text: During Alghero’s plague outbreak of 1582 to 1583, the physician Quinto Tiberio Angelerio organized restrictions later published as fifty-seven instructions. One rule allowed only one member of a household to go shopping, with permission. Another required people outside to carry a six-foot cane to keep their distance.

The rules also told physicians to visit patients regardless of wealth: richer people would pay, while the city would cover poor patients. Pharmacies had to maintain supplies. These prescriptions show an effort to organize public help during a crisis, although the surviving rules cannot prove that every patient received it.

Some prescriptions came from mistaken explanations of disease: bells and artillery were supposed to purify the air. The same programme used isolation and heated objects and textiles. Angelerio worked before the bacterium and flea transmission were understood; his booklet combined observation with the medical ideas of his time.

Teeth offer a different window into life. Researchers examined 160 people from Alghero’s plague cemetery, including 79 children or adolescents. Cavities, tartar and tooth loss suggested substantial carbohydrate consumption and poor oral hygiene. This is an inference from one burial population, not a menu for every Sardinian family.

ending.text: The map ends in 1700, but Spanish rule did not instantly end then. Sardinia passed to Austrian control in 1708, was retaken by Spain in 1717, and came under the House of Savoy in 1720. Its institutions and communities continued through these changes of dynasty.
